name: Neva Green
lede: Neva Green is a muted yellow-green named for the Neva, the short, fast river that carries Lake Ladoga's water through Saint Petersburg to the Gulf of Finland.

sections.title: A river's name
sections.body:
The Neva runs only about 74 kilometers, yet carries more water than any other river in Europe apart from the Volga, Danube and a handful of others, draining the whole Ladoga basin in its short course [3]. Ridgway's 1912 color standards plate this green on plate V, hue 29, and the ISCC-NBS dictionary of 1955 later filed the same swatch as a brilliant yellowish green, 6.9 units from that block's center [1]. Maerz and Paul's dictionary gives 1912 as the color's first recorded use and the Munsell notation 4.4GY 7.0/6.8 [1].

Its nearest named neighbors are Light Olive, 2.6 units away, and Absinthe Green, 3.1 units away [1]. It sits in the same olive-green cluster as [[light-olive]] and the broader family of [[green]], without a sibling color sharing its own place-name [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color within six units of Neva Green covers at least five percent of the canvas in only 35 works, about fifteen hundredths of one percent[2]. The earliest dated example is Lucas Cranach's 1548 portrait of a man, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [2]. It peaks in the 1870s, in 6 of 1,065 paintings, nearly four times the archive's overall rate for that decade, and it turns up in Impressionist paintings fifteen times the baseline rate [2]. Fifty-seven percent of its appearances sit in a painting's highlights rather than its mid-tones or shadows [2]. It shares a canvas with [[khaki]] more than any other color word, eighteen times the baseline [2]. These are screen-color matches on photographs of aged, varnished paintings, not pigment identifications [2]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, read as screen colors, not pigment identifications[2].
